name: Uma Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential and won't have your name on it. Could you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker with the regional power company, and right now I'm on the street lighting and maintenance crew. So I spend a lot of the day up in a bucket truck, that's the truck with the arm and the basket, swapping old street lamps for LED ones and fixing faults on the lines along the main roads. We cover our town and three others in the valley, so there's a lot of driving between jobs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can drive down River Road at night and see the lights I put up. My grandfather would have loved that. What wears me out is that I'm still slow with the hydraulics and the controls in the bucket, and my supervisor, Mr Okafor, has to talk me through things I should know by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's good, people can get on with their lives. At family dinners I'd say I'm glad my fiancé's job is safe. I don't post much online, maybe something on the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means our plans stay on track. Yusuf and I are getting married next autumn, and we're saving for the wedding and a deposit on a small house. I'd much rather spend the next year arguing about the guest list than about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are. I've got about four months of savings in my own account and we're putting money aside together each month. I'd keep using the AI app Yusuf showed me now and then, mostly to help write things for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Yusuf do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a bookkeeper at a farm supply company in town. He's the one who uses all the computer things, I only use what he shows me once he's sure it works. He jokes that he's the tech department of our relationship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe that we'd spent so much time worrying for nothing. My mother has been praying about Yusuf's job for a year because of all the news.

S0.say: I'd say that's good, people can get on with their lives. At family dinners I'd say I'm glad my fiancé's job is safe.
S0.think: It means our plans stay on track: the wedding next autumn and saving for a small house. I'd rather spend the year arguing about the guest list than about robots.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, holding about four months of savings and saving jointly with her fiancé each month. Keeps using an AI app now and then for work writing.
S0.quote: I'd much rather spend the next year arguing about the guest list than about robots.
S0.fieldNote: Uma sees the future through her household, and her fiancé's office job is the one the family worries about, not hers. She adopts technology once he's tested it, which fits her steady nature. Faith and family run quietly through the answers, from her mother's prayers to her grandfather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard and learn what they need to, and companies should train their own people instead of throwing them out. At the community centre I'd say families need to help each other through it. I don't think the government should just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about me. Lines and street lights still need people. It's Yusuf I'd be lying awake about, because a computer can already do half his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding date, but we'd plan a smaller reception and put the difference, maybe a few thousand, into savings. I'd encourage Yusuf to learn new skills while he still has his job. For myself I'd keep going and learn the new tools at work once the others are using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a smaller wedding cause any trouble in the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, yes. My aunts have a list of two hundred people. I'd have to explain to my aunts that robots are the reason they're not invited. My mother would back me, though, she's very sensible about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skills would you want Yusuf to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's said he might like the accounting side for small businesses, the advice part, not the typing in numbers. I'd tell him to ask his company to pay for a course. That's what a good employer does.

S1.say: I'd say people should work hard and learn what they need, and companies should train their own people. Families need to help each other, rather than waiting for government money.
S1.think: I'm not worried about me, because lines and street lights still need people. It's Yusuf I'd lie awake about, because a computer can already do half his job.
S1.do: Keeps the wedding date but plans a smaller reception and moves a few thousand into savings. Encourages her fiancé to retrain while employed and learns new work tools once colleagues use them.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not for herself but for the two of them.
S1.quote: I'd have to explain to my aunts that robots are the reason they're not invited.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is entirely about her fiancé's exposed office job, which flips the usual expectation that the hands-on worker is at risk. The smaller wedding is her concrete lever, and she expects a family row over it. She believes firmly that employers should pay for retraining rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pull together as families and communities, because nobody else is ready. I'd say the companies owe it to their workers to keep them as long as they can. I wouldn't be shouting about it, it's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, both of us would be in trouble. Yusuf's job would go first, maybe in months, and two years later robots could be doing mine. We'd be a young couple starting out with nothing certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd move the wedding up and make it small, just family at the mosque and a meal at my parents' house. We'd put the house deposit on hold and live with my parents for a while to save, they've already offered. I'd keep working every shift I could and add to the savings while I still have pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be holding it together for Yusuf, but inside I'd be shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move the wedding up rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything is falling apart, I'd want us to be married and facing it together. Waiting for things to be perfect makes no sense when nothing will be. My grandmother married during a war. She'd tell me a wedding doesn't need a hall, it needs two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel living with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grateful, and a bit squashed. My father would want to know what time we come home, like I'm sixteen. But family is what it's for, I'd never be too proud to accept it.

S2.say: I'd say we need to pull together as families and communities because nobody else is ready. Companies owe it to their workers to keep them as long as they can.
S2.think: Both of us would be in trouble: Yusuf's job would go within months and robots could be doing mine two years later. We'd be a young couple starting out with nothing certain.
S2.do: Brings the wedding forward as a small family event at the mosque and her parents' house, and puts the house deposit on hold. Moves in with her parents to save and works every available shift.
S2.feel: Alarmed, holding it together for her fiancé while shaking inside.
S2.quote: My grandmother married during a war. She'd tell me a wedding doesn't need a hall, it needs two people.
S2.fieldNote: Uma's instinct under pressure is to move closer to family, not further: marry sooner, move home, share costs. The threat is doubled because both incomes are exposed on different timelines. Her grandmother's wartime wedding gives her a model for getting through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for companies to train their people properly, through apprenticeships, not just online videos. I'd say it to Mr Okafor and anyone at the company who'd listen. People learn trades by working next to someone who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be properly qualified and we'd have a few years of two incomes, if Yusuf moves into something safer. It'd be tight, but we could still have our wedding and maybe even the house. But I'd always know there's a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding as planned but small, and wait a year on the house to see how things go. I'd ask the company if they run any training for the jobs that work alongside the robots, like checking and repairing them, and I'd sign up once others have tried it. Yusuf would start his small-business advice course this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I can see a path, if I squint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign up once others had tried it. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen courses that were a waste of time. Last year the company sent two guys on a smart meter course, and then they never used it. I'd rather be second in line for something that works than first in line for something that doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the five years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd always said two or three years after the wedding. With five years warning, I think we'd still try, but we'd want more saved first. My mother would say children are a blessing, not a budget line.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for companies to train people properly through apprenticeships, not online videos. People learn trades by working next to someone who knows.
S3.think: Five years means I'd qualify and we'd have a few years of two incomes if Yusuf moves somewhere safer. We could still have the wedding and maybe the house, but there'd always be a deadline.
S3.do: Keeps a small wedding as planned and delays the house by a year. Signs up for company training in robot checking and repair once others have tried it, while her fiancé starts a small-business advice course.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to see a path.
S3.quote: I'd rather be second in line for something that works than first in line for something that doesn't.
S3.fieldNote: Her steady style is explicit: she'd be second in line for proven training, not first. She frames retraining as an apprenticeship model rather than online learning. Children come up as something they'd still plan, just with more savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and everyone should use it, families, churches, mosques, companies. I'd say young people should learn a trade properly, because hands-on work will still be the last to go. I'd say it at the community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a normal life for a while. Married, a house, maybe a child, and a job I'm actually good at by then. I'd want ten good years and then I'd want to know my children won't be raised by a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, buy the house in two years and keep saving as usual. In five or six years, once I'd seen what the robot work looks like, I'd do whatever training the company offers. I'd keep using the AI tools a bit more, the way Yusuf does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry at the back of my mind, but I can still plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your children won't be raised by a screen. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean if nobody has jobs, everybody's at home on their phones. I want my kids to see their parents go to work and come home tired. That matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change how you think about Yusuf's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. He'd have time to move into the advice side and build up his own clients. Honestly, in ten years I think he'd adapt faster than me, he's always been the one who reads the instructions.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and everyone should use it, from families and mosques to companies. Young people should learn a trade properly because hands-on work will be the last to go.
S4.think: Ten years feels like a normal life for a while: married, a house, maybe a child and a job I'm good at. I'd want ten good years and then to know my children won't be raised by a screen.
S4.do: Holds the wedding as planned, buys a house in about two years and keeps saving. Takes company training in five or six years once robot work is clearer and uses AI tools a little more often.
S4.feel: Uneasy, a worry in the background while she plans a life.
S4.quote: Honestly, in ten years I think he'd adapt faster than me, he's always been the one who reads the instructions.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Uma returns to her original plans almost unchanged. Her deeper worry is cultural rather than financial: children growing up without seeing parents go to work. She expects her fiancé to adapt faster than she would.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Yusuf and I would both lose our footing at the same time, right when we're starting our life together. What would help is companies keeping on their apprentices and training them into the new jobs, and families and communities sticking together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people believe in. When work goes, a lot of people lose their reason to get up. Faith and family give you that, but not everybody has them, and I worry about the people who don't.

headlineQuote: I'd want ten good years and then I'd want to know my children won't be raised by a screen.
portrait: Uma is a 27-year-old junior lineworker on a street lighting crew for a regional power company, still slow with the bucket truck controls, engaged to Yusuf, a bookkeeper, with a wedding planned for next autumn. She uses AI tools only after he's tried them and prefers proven training to being first in line. She's calm about the plateau and uneasy in steady disruption, worried mostly about Yusuf's office job. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both incomes would go, and she'd marry sooner and move in with her parents. With more warning she keeps her plans, takes employer training when it's proven and worries more about what a world without work means for family and faith.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her fiancé would both lose their footing just as they start their life together.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping their apprentices and training them into new jobs, along with families and communities sticking together.
